name: Gunmetal
lede: Gunmetal is the dark blue-grey of the alloy once used for cannon and gun parts, and it is now a standard word for a cool, dark grey.

sections.title: The metal and the color
sections.body:
Paterson defines gunmetal as the dull blue-grey of the metal, a dark grey, and notes the variant gunmetal blue [1]. St Clair's glossary of color words gives it a similar gloss, mid-blue-grey [2]. The two differ in lightness, with one calling it dark and the other mid, which suggests a loose word rather than a fixed standard [1][2].

In Paterson's index it sits among the greys with granite, graphite, iron grey and slate [3]. Close neighbors in our names are [[slate-grey]], [[charcoal]] and [[dark-slate-grey]].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch is a very dark, cool grey with a slight blue-green cast. Real gunmetal varies by alloy and finish, so a screen sample is a convention only [1]. Our own library also lists Japanese traditional colors whose nearest match is this name, such as the iron-color tetsu-iro, which is a separate tradition and not a translation [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch matches 762 of 23,781 archive paintings (3.2%, as photographed), more common than 82% of the named colors [5]. It peaks in the 1200s, in 4.2% of the 142 paintings from then, about 1.9 times the expected rate, but that is only 6 paintings [5]. Inside a painting it most often plays a mid-tone, in 48% of the 467 paintings that hold it, and the most devoted painter is Fra Angelico, in 5 of 16 works here [5]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test.
